questions.stem: A 5 year old girl has a 3 day history of pain in her right lower leg and refuses to walk. There is no history of injury. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg. There is warmth and point tenderness over the distal tibia. CRP is 96 mg/L. MRI shows marrow oedema in the distal tibial metaphysis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of osteomyelitis in all children; Salmonella is the classic organism only in sickle cell disease.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Haematogenous osteomyelitis of a long-bone **metaphysis** in a child: commonest organism in **all** children is **S. aureus**.

elim: A neonatal and urinary organism, not the usual cause in a school-age child.
Now rare since vaccination.
Linked to puncture wounds through footwear, not haematogenous spread.
Characteristic in sickle cell disease, which she does not have.

steps.x: **E. Staphylococcus aureus.** Osteomyelitis organism = S. aureus unless sickle cell (Salmonella).

questions.stem: A 10 year old boy has a 4 day history of pain around his right knee and a limp. He has a fever. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg. The knee joint moves fully without pain but there is marked bony tenderness just above it. CRP is 110 mg/L.
questions.q: Which part of the femur is most likely to be infected?
questions.e: In children, haematogenous osteomyelitis most commonly affects the metaphysis of a long bone, where blood flow is rich but sluggish.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which part of the femur is most likely to be infected? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: knee joint moves fully without pain
steps.x: Full painless joint movement with bone tenderness **near** the joint = bone, not joint. Children seed the **metaphysis**.

elim: The shaft is not the usual site of haematogenous osteomyelitis in children.
Less often affected; the growth plate is a barrier in older children.
Would cause hip, not knee, pain.
Periosteal elevation is a consequence, not the primary site.

steps.x: **D. Metaphysis.** Child long bone osteomyelitis = metaphysis.

questions.stem: A 68 year old man had open reduction and internal fixation of a fractured right ankle 6 weeks ago. He now has constant pain over the lateral malleolus, worse at night and on weight-bearing, with redness over the plate. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 134/80 mmHg. CRP is 148 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Recent fracture surgery is a major risk factor; localised bone pain worse with activity and at night with fever and raised CRP is osteomyelitis.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: internal fixation of a fractured right ankle 6 weeks ago
worse at night and on weight-bearing
steps.x: **Recent surgical repair** plus localised bone pain worse at **night** and on activity, fever and raised CRP.

elim: Skin infection alone does not explain deep bone pain worse at night after metalwork.
Pain, swelling and colour change without fever or raised CRP.
Calf swelling, not focal bone pain over a plate with fever.
Painful but not febrile with a CRP of 148.

steps.x: **E. Osteomyelitis.** Bone pain + fever + recent surgery or open fracture = osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man with type 2 diabetes has a 4 week history of constant lower back pain, worse at night, with sweats. His temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. Leg power, sensation and reflexes are normal and he has no bladder symptoms. CRP is 132 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his back?
o: Tenderness to percussion over a vertebra
questions.e: In vertebral osteomyelitis neurological symptoms are not typical, but local tenderness to spinal percussion may be found.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his back? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Leg power, sensation and reflexes are normal
steps.x: Diabetic man, night pain, fever, raised CRP = **vertebral osteomyelitis**. Neuro signs are **not typical**; expect **percussion tenderness**.

elim: Neurological symptoms are not typical unless an epidural abscess develops.
Suggests a lumbar disc prolapse.
Ankylosing spondylitis.
Cauda equina syndrome.

steps.x: **E. Tenderness to percussion over a vertebra.** Vertebral osteomyelitis: spinal percussion tenderness, normal neurology.

questions.stem: A 14 year old boy with sickle cell disease has a 5 day history of left hip pain and fever. He usually has bone pain in crises, but this pain has not settled with his normal analgesia. His temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 118 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. The left hip is warm, tender and red. CRP is 188 mg/L. MRI shows bone marrow oedema of the femoral head with a periosteal collection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
questions.e: In sickle cell disease osteomyelitis classically affects the femoral or humeral head with fever and a warm, tender, red joint; a crisis usually settles with analgesia.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: has not settled with his normal analgesia
steps.x: **Sickle cell** + fever + warm, tender, red joint region + marrow oedema with a collection = osteomyelitis of the **femoral head**.

elim: Causes hip pain in sickle cell, but without high fever, erythema and a periosteal collection.
Idiopathic avascular necrosis in younger children, without fever.
A mechanical slip, not febrile.
Settles with analgesia and does not cause a periosteal collection.

steps.x: **B. Osteomyelitis of the femoral head.** Sickle cell + persistent fever and bone pain = think osteomyelitis (Salmonella).

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy was treated for osteomyelitis of the left femur 6 weeks ago but stopped his oral antibiotics after a few days. Today he had sudden severe thigh pain after a minor trip and cannot stand. His temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. The thigh is deformed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
o: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
questions.e: Complications of osteomyelitis include chronic osteomyelitis, sepsis, bone destruction and pathological fracture through weakened bone.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely complication? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: stopped his oral antibiotics after a few days
steps.x: Untreated osteomyelitis **destroys bone**, so it breaks with **minor trauma**: a pathological fracture.

elim: Gives hip pain and limp, not a deformed thigh after a trip.
Severe pain on passive stretch after a crush or tight cast.
A tumour, not a complication of osteomyelitis.
A hot, swollen joint without deformity of the thigh.

steps.x: **D. Pathological fracture.** Osteomyelitis complications: chronic infection, sepsis, bone destruction, pathological fracture.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man had an open tibial fracture 6 years ago. He has had a discharging opening on his shin on and off for 4 years. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. CRP is 34 mg/L. An X-ray of the tibia is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray?
o: Dead bone fragment surrounded by thick new bone
questions.e: Chronic osteomyelitis forms a sequestrum of dead infected bone surrounded by involucrum, with a discharging sinus.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: discharging opening on his shin on and off for 4 years
steps.x: **Chronic osteomyelitis**: a **sequestrum** (dead bone) inside an **involucrum** (reactive new bone), with a sinus.

elim: Calcified cartilage of pseudogout.
Classic for Ewing's sarcoma.
Chronic infection over years leaves visible bone changes.
Giant cell tumour.

steps.x: **B. Dead bone fragment surrounded by thick new bone.** Chronic osteomyelitis X-ray = sequestrum + involucrum.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl has a 2 day history of pain in her left distal femur and fever. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 122 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. There is point tenderness over the distal femur. CRP is 84 mg/L. An X-ray of the femur is taken in the emergency department.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray?
questions.e: X-ray is often normal early in osteomyelitis because cortical destruction and periosteal reaction appear later; MRI shows early marrow oedema.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on X-ray? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Only **2 days** of illness. X-ray changes (cortical destruction, periosteal reaction) are a **later** finding.

elim: Takes 10 to 14 days or more to appear on X-ray.
A later X-ray finding.
Chronic osteomyelitis after months.
Osteosarcoma.

steps.x: **B. No bony abnormality.** Early osteomyelitis: X-ray normal; MRI positive.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with paraplegia from a spinal cord injury has a deep sacral pressure ulcer. Bone is visible at its base and there is foul discharge. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. CRP is 176 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Prior spinal injury and necrotic ulcers are risk factors; infection spreads from the ulcer into the underlying bone.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Bone is visible at its base
steps.x: **Prior spinal injury** with a necrotic ulcer reaching **bone**: contiguous spread into bone.

elim: Inflammatory back pain in young men, not an infected ulcer.
Does not explain exposed bone at the base of a deep ulcer.
Natal cleft sinus in young hairy adults.
Bone pain without an infected ulcer over it.

steps.x: **C. Osteomyelitis of the sacrum.** Ulcer down to bone = osteomyelitis until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: A 10 year old girl has a 3 day history of pain in her right upper arm and will not lift it. She has a fever. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. There is swelling and redness over the proximal humerus with marked bony tenderness. The shoulder can be moved passively with only mild discomfort. CRP is 140 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Acute osteomyelitis gives localised bone pain and tenderness, fever, swelling, erythema, reduced limb use and raised CRP; septic arthritis prevents any joint movement.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: moved passively with only mild discomfort
steps.x: Acute fever, local **bone** tenderness, swelling and redness, **reduced limb use**, raised CRP, but the joint moves.

elim: Can cause fever and bone pain, but develops over weeks to months.
Chronic joint swelling with stiffness, not acute bone tenderness with high fever.
The shoulder would be very painful to move at all.
Follows a fall and affects the elbow.

steps.x: **A. Acute osteomyelitis.** Bone tender, joint moves = osteomyelitis; joint frozen = septic arthritis.

questions.stem: A 63 year old woman on haemodialysis through a tunnelled line had Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia 3 weeks ago. She now has thoracic back pain, worse at night. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 146/84 mmHg. She is tender over T10. Neurological examination is normal. CRP is 122 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Haematogenous seeding after S. aureus bacteraemia causes vertebral osteomyelitis with night pain, fever and focal spinal tenderness.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Recent **S. aureus bacteraemia** seeds the spine. Night pain, fever, focal tenderness, raised CRP.

elim: Starts in young adults with morning stiffness, not after bacteraemia.
Neurology is normal and there is a clear infective source.
Sudden pain after minor trauma, without fever.
Loin pain with urinary symptoms, not spinal tenderness.

steps.x: **E. Vertebral osteomyelitis.** Bacteraemia + new back pain = vertebral osteomyelitis.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman who injects heroin into her groin has a 1 week history of pain and swelling over her left tibia. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 108 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg. There is warmth and bony tenderness over the tibial shaft. CRP is 158 mg/L. MRI confirms osteomyelitis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of osteomyelitis, including in people who inject drugs.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: bony tenderness over the tibial shaft
steps.x: **IV drug use** is a risk factor. The commonest osteomyelitis organism overall is **S. aureus**.

elim: Causes slow spinal disease (Pott's), not an acute week-long tibial infection.
Possible in drug users, but not the commonest cause.
Classic in sickle cell disease.
A respiratory organism, rarely a cause of bone infection.

steps.x: **D. Staphylococcus aureus.** Default organism = S. aureus.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man with type 2 diabetes and peripheral neuropathy had a heel pressure ulcer that healed 2 months ago. He now has constant right heel pain, worse at night, and feels feverish. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 144/86 mmHg. The heel is warm and tender. CRP is 98 mg/L and an X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Diabetes and foot ulcers are major risk factors; bone pain worse at night with fever and raised CRP suggests osteomyelitis even if the X-ray is normal.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely diagnosis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Diabetes** with a previous ulcer, night pain, fever, raised CRP. A normal X-ray does **not** exclude it early.

elim: Pain above the heel on activity, without fever.
A warm swollen midfoot without fever or very high CRP.
Sudden attacks of a hot joint, usually the first MTP.
Pain on first steps in the morning, not constant night pain with fever.

steps.x: **D. Osteomyelitis of the calcaneus.** Diabetic foot + night pain + raised CRP = osteomyelitis; X-ray may be normal.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has had acute osteomyelitis of the right tibia diagnosed 1 day ago and is waiting for antibiotics to be started. He is now drowsy and mottled. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 168 bpm, BP 72/40 mmHg and capillary refill time 5 seconds. Lactate is 4.6 mmol/L.
questions.q: Which is the most likely complication?
questions.e: Sepsis is a complication of osteomyelitis; signs of systemic illness mean sepsis must be considered and managed urgently.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely complication? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Hypotension, tachycardia, poor perfusion, raised lactate in a child with bone infection = **sepsis**.

elim: Develops over months, not in a day.
Severe limb pain without shock and lactic acidosis.
Causes a deformed limb, not shock.
Causes a hot knee, not this circulatory failure on its own.

steps.x: **D. Sepsis.** Osteomyelitis + shock = sepsis.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has a 5 day history of pain and swelling over her right tibia after a deep puncture wound from a garden fork. She has not had antibiotics. Her temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 122/76 mmHg. The tibia is tender and red.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Initial investigations for osteomyelitis are bloods (CRP, ESR, WBC), blood cultures taken before antibiotics, and imaging.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
First-line: **bloods** (CRP, ESR, WBC) and **blood cultures** before antibiotics, plus imaging.

elim: Not a first-line test.
Not first-line; MRI is the sensitive imaging test.
Measures bone density.
Tests for gout.

steps.x: **A. Blood cultures.** Febrile bone infection: blood cultures before antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 49 year old man who injects drugs has a 3 week history of lower back pain, worse at night, and fevers. He is tender over L3. Leg neurology is normal. His temperature is 38.1°C, pulse rate 100 bpm and BP 126/78 mmHg. CRP is 120 mg/L and lumbar spine X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation?
questions.e: MRI is the most sensitive early investigation for osteomyelitis, showing bone marrow oedema; X-ray changes appear later.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate imaging investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Suspected vertebral osteomyelitis with a **normal X-ray**: **MRI** is the most sensitive early test.

elim: Less specific than MRI.
Not the best test for vertebral bone and disc infection.
Delays diagnosis; X-ray changes come late.
Cannot assess the vertebral marrow.

steps.x: **C. MRI of the spine.** Suspected osteomyelitis, normal X-ray = MRI.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy has a 2 day history of pain in his left lower leg and fever. His temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg. There is tenderness over the proximal tibia. X-ray is normal. An ultrasound scan of the tibia is performed while waiting for MRI.
questions.q: Which finding on ultrasound most suggests osteomyelitis?
o: Subperiosteal fluid collection over 4 mm deep
questions.e: On ultrasound, a subperiosteal fluid collection more than 4 mm deep suggests osteomyelitis; MRI remains the most sensitive test.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which finding on ultrasound most suggests osteomyelitis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Ultrasound: a **subperiosteal** collection **deeper than 4 mm** suggests osteomyelitis.

elim: Suggests a joint problem, not bone.
Does not suggest infection.
A Baker's cyst behind the knee.
Tendinopathy.

steps.x: **D. Subperiosteal fluid collection over 4 mm deep.** Ultrasound sign = subperiosteal collection over 4 mm.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has vertebral osteomyelitis of L2 on MRI. She is clinically stable and has not been given antibiotics. Two sets of blood cultures are negative. Her temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 136/80 mmHg. CRP is 82 mg/L.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
o: Repeat blood cultures daily for a week
questions.e: Bone biopsy for histology and culture is the gold standard and guides antibiotic choice; in a stable patient antibiotics can await the result.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate next investigation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**Bone biopsy** for pathology and culture is the gold standard and **guides definitive antibiotics**. Stable patient: wait for it.

elim: Adds nothing; diagnosis is already shown on MRI.
Risks spreading infection and does not sample the bone.
Not needed and does not identify the organism.
Delays diagnosis; bone tissue gives the organism.

steps.x: **B. CT-guided biopsy of the vertebra.** Stable, cultures negative = biopsy before antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man is on day 10 of IV flucloxacillin and rifampicin for tibial osteomyelitis. He feels better and his fever has settled. His temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg. The team wants a blood test to monitor his response to treatment.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor his response?
questions.e: CRP and ESR are raised in osteomyelitis; serial CRP is used to monitor response because it falls quickly when treatment works.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to monitor his response? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: day 10 of IV flucloxacillin and rifampicin
steps.x: CRP is raised in osteomyelitis and **falls** as infection settles, so serial **CRP** tracks response.

elim: A bone turnover marker that does not track infection.
Used to diagnose bacteraemia, not to monitor response.
Not routinely used to monitor bone infection.
Not a marker of infection.

steps.x: **C. C-reactive protein.** Monitor osteomyelitis treatment with CRP.

questions.stem: A 12 year old boy was diagnosed with osteomyelitis of the distal radius 3 weeks ago but did not attend follow-up or take his antibiotics. He still has wrist pain and swelling. His temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 96 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. His initial X-ray was normal. A new X-ray is taken.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on the new X-ray?
questions.e: X-ray shows cortical destruction and periosteal reaction as a later finding in osteomyelitis, often normal in the first 1 to 2 weeks.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely finding on the new X-ray? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: did not attend follow-up or take his antibiotics
steps.x: X-ray signs come **later**: after weeks, **cortical destruction** and **periosteal reaction** appear.

elim: Pseudogout.
By 3 weeks changes are usually visible.
Osteoarthritis.
Giant cell tumour.

steps.x: **D. Periosteal reaction with cortical destruction.** X-ray changes in osteomyelitis are late: periosteal reaction, cortical destruction.

questions.stem: An 11 year old girl with sickle cell disease has a 4 day history of right shoulder pain and fever. Her pain has not improved with opioids as her crises normally do. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 106/66 mmHg. The shoulder is warm and tender. CRP is 164 mg/L and X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to distinguish infection from a crisis?
questions.e: MRI is the most sensitive early test for osteomyelitis and shows marrow oedema with periosteal elevation; in sickle cell disease the humeral and femoral heads are typical sites.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate investigation to distinguish infection from a crisis? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Sickle cell + humeral head pain + persisting fever = possible osteomyelitis. **MRI** is the most sensitive early test.

elim: Bone infarction and infection both take up tracer.
Less sensitive for early marrow changes.
Confirms sickle cell disease, which is already known.
Delays diagnosis; X-ray changes are late.

steps.x: **D. MRI of the humerus.** Suspected osteomyelitis with a normal X-ray = MRI.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has osteomyelitis of the left tibia around the plate fixing an open fracture 2 months ago. Blood cultures are negative and a superficial wound swab grew skin flora. He is stable. His temperature is 37.7°C, pulse rate 86 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. He is listed for debridement.
questions.q: Which investigation is most likely to identify the causative organism?
o: Deep bone samples taken at debridement for culture
questions.e: Bone biopsy samples for histology and culture identify the organism and guide definitive therapy; superficial swabs are unreliable.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which investigation is most likely to identify the causative organism? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: superficial wound swab grew skin flora
steps.x: Gold standard = **bone biopsy** for pathology and culture. Superficial swabs grow **colonisers**.

elim: Already negative and often negative in post-traumatic infection.
Grows colonising skin flora, not the bone organism.
Does not identify an organism.
Not relevant to bone infection.

steps.x: **A. Deep bone samples taken at debridement for culture.** Organism in osteomyelitis = bone biopsy culture.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has acute osteomyelitis of the right tibia confirmed on MRI. He has started IV flucloxacillin and rifampicin and is improving. He has no allergies. His temperature is 37.4°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 130/78 mmHg. He asks how long his antibiotics will last.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate total duration of antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: Acute osteomyelitis needs flucloxacillin with rifampicin for at least 4 weeks, with a total course of 4 to 6 weeks, IV then tailored.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate total duration of antibiotic treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: acute osteomyelitis of the right tibia
steps.x: Empirical **IV flucloxacillin + rifampicin** for at least **4 weeks**, total course **4 to 6 weeks**.

elim: Far too short for bone infection.
Excessive for acute osteomyelitis.
Too short; at least 4 weeks is needed.
Far too short.

steps.x: **E. 4 to 6 weeks.** Osteomyelitis antibiotics: 4 to 6 weeks.

questions.stem: A 47 year old woman has acute osteomyelitis of the left fibula. She takes warfarin for a mechanical heart valve and the team wants to avoid a drug that strongly induces liver enzymes. She has no allergies. Her temperature is 38.2°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?
questions.e: Empirical treatment is IV flucloxacillin with rifampicin, and fusidic acid can replace rifampicin, for example when rifampicin interactions are a problem.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: avoid a drug that strongly induces liver enzymes
steps.x: Empirical treatment is flucloxacillin + rifampicin, but **fusidic acid can replace rifampicin**, here because of warfarin.

elim: Rifampicin is a potent enzyme inducer and would lower her INR.
Kept for confirmed MRSA.
Poor anti-staphylococcal cover for bone.
For severe penicillin allergy; she has none.

steps.x: **A. IV flucloxacillin and fusidic acid.** Flucloxacillin + rifampicin (or fusidic acid).

questions.stem: A 38 year old man has acute osteomyelitis of the right femur. Two years ago he developed lip and tongue swelling and wheeze within minutes of a dose of amoxicillin. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Blood cultures have been taken.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic?
questions.e: Clindamycin is used for osteomyelitis in severe penicillin allergy; all penicillins, including flucloxacillin, must be avoided.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: lip and tongue swelling and wheeze within minutes of a dose of amoxicillin
steps.x: Angioedema and wheeze = **severe penicillin allergy**, so no flucloxacillin. Use **clindamycin**.

elim: Contains a penicillin.
A penicillin; contraindicated after anaphylaxis.
A penicillin.
Contains a penicillin.

steps.x: **A. Clindamycin.** Severe penicillin allergy = clindamycin.

questions.stem: An 82 year old care home resident has osteomyelitis of the left calcaneus under a pressure ulcer. She has been on IV flucloxacillin and rifampicin. Bone biopsy grows meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus sensitive to glycopeptides. Her temperature is 37.9°C, pulse rate 92 bpm and BP 128/74 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic?
questions.e: Vancomycin is used when MRSA is confirmed on bone biopsy; flucloxacillin does not cover meticillin-resistant organisms.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**MRSA** confirmed on biopsy = switch to **vancomycin**.

elim: Has no activity against MRSA.
Has no activity against MRSA.
MRSA is resistant whatever the dose.
Covers anaerobes only.

steps.x: **E. Vancomycin.** MRSA osteomyelitis = vancomycin.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has had a discharging sinus over his left tibia for 3 years after an open fracture. He is systemically well. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 76 bpm and BP 138/84 mmHg. CRP is 28 mg/L. X-ray shows a sequestrum. He has not taken antibiotics recently.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate approach to antibiotic treatment?
o: Await culture and sensitivities from bone samples
Treat based on a sinus swab
questions.e: In chronic osteomyelitis, antimicrobials should await culture and sensitivities from bone samples, usually taken at surgical debridement.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate approach to antibiotic treatment? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: discharging sinus over his left tibia for 3 years
steps.x: **Chronic osteomyelitis** in a well patient: antimicrobials should **await sensitivities**.

elim: Blind treatment rarely clears chronic infection and hides the organism.
No MRSA has been shown and he is well.
Wrong spectrum and blind.
Sinus swabs grow colonisers, not the bone organism.

steps.x: **A. Await culture and sensitivities from bone samples.** Chronic osteomyelitis, stable = sample first, then treat.

questions.stem: A 45 year old woman has chronic osteomyelitis of the right tibia with a sinus for 2 years. Several courses of antibiotics have failed. X-ray and MRI show a large sequestrum surrounded by involucrum. Her temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 130/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Further 6 weeks of IV antibiotics alone
questions.e: Chronic osteomyelitis with a sequestrum needs surgical debridement combined with culture-guided antibiotics; antibiotics alone cannot reach dead bone.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate definitive management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: Several courses of antibiotics have failed
steps.x: Dead infected bone (**sequestrum**) has no blood supply. Needs **surgical debridement** plus antibiotics.

elim: Only for extensive, unreconstructable disease.
Antibiotics cannot penetrate a sequestrum.
Not definitive treatment.
Do not reach the dead bone.

steps.x: **E. Surgical debridement with targeted antibiotics.** Sequestrum = surgery plus antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a foot ulcer over the 1st metatarsal head. MRI shows osteomyelitis with a 3 cm abscess in the plantar soft tissues. The foot is red and swollen with pus from the ulcer. Her temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 128/78 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: IV antibiotics and urgent surgical drainage
Oral antibiotics and review in 2 weeks
questions.e: Diabetic foot osteomyelitis with a deep abscess requires surgical drainage alongside IV antibiotics; antibiotics alone fail.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most appropriate management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: 3 cm abscess in the plantar soft tissues
steps.x: **Diabetic foot ulcer + deep abscess** needs **surgical drainage** alongside antibiotics.

elim: Do not treat a deep abscess.
Will not clear an abscess.
Inadequate for a febrile deep foot infection.
For Charcot foot, not infection.

steps.x: **C. IV antibiotics and urgent surgical drainage.** Diabetic foot abscess = drain it.

questions.stem: A 72 year old man with osteomyelitis of the left tibia becomes confused on the ward. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 124 bpm, BP 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air. Lactate is 4.2 mmol/L. Antibiotics are due in 6 hours.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Await bone biopsy results before antibiotics
Blood cultures, then IV antibiotics and fluids within 1 hour
Give the next antibiotic dose when due
questions.e: With systemic illness, sepsis must be recognised and managed: blood cultures, then IV antibiotics and fluids within an hour, without waiting for biopsy.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the next most appropriate step in management? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Hypotension and lactate over 4 = **sepsis**. Sepsis six within 1 hour: cultures, IV antibiotics, fluids, oxygen, lactate, urine output.

elim: Unsafe in sepsis; antibiotics must not be delayed.
Delays treatment by 6 hours in septic shock.
Inadequate for septic shock.
Imaging does not resuscitate him.

steps.x: **B. Blood cultures, then IV antibiotics and fluids within 1 hour.** Septic patient = sepsis six now.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman develops osteomyelitis of the proximal tibia 4 weeks after a tibial plateau fracture was fixed with a plate and screws. She has no other source of infection and blood cultures are negative. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 94 bpm and BP 132/80 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of infection?
o: Contiguous spread from a foot ulcer
questions.e: Osteomyelitis arises from haematogenous seeding of the metaphysis, mainly in children, or from direct inoculation through trauma, surgery or a contiguous ulcer.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely route of infection? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: fixed with a plate and screws
steps.x: After fracture fixation bacteria enter **directly** at the time of trauma or **surgery**.

elim: No ulcer is present.
The typical route in children, not after open fixation with no bacteraemia.
Not a route of bone infection.
The sickle cell Salmonella mechanism.

steps.x: **B. Direct inoculation at surgery.** Adults after surgery: direct inoculation. Children: haematogenous.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man has osteomyelitis around a tibial nail. He asks why he needs many weeks of antibiotics and may need the metalwork removed. Bone biopsy grew Staphylococcus aureus. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 82 bpm and BP 136/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Bacteria form a biofilm on bone and metal
Staphylococcus aureus is resistant to all antibiotics
The antibiotics are destroyed in bone
questions.e: S. aureus adhesins bind bone matrix and implants and form biofilms that impair antibiotic penetration and immune clearance, so long courses and often surgery are needed.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
**S. aureus adhesins** bind bone matrix proteins and form **biofilms** that block antibiotic penetration and immune clearance.

elim: Not the main reason for long courses.
Living bone is vascular; the issue is biofilm and dead bone.
It is sensitive to flucloxacillin here.
Not the mechanism.

steps.x: **B. Bacteria form a biofilm on bone and metal.** Biofilm = long antibiotics, sometimes surgery.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman with sickle cell disease has osteomyelitis of the left humeral head. Blood cultures grow Salmonella. She had severe abdominal pain during a crisis a week earlier. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 108/68 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her infection?
o: Bowel infarction allowing gut organisms into the blood
Direct spread from an infected skin ulcer
Hyposplenism reducing cover against Staphylococcus aureus only
questions.e: In sickle cell disease, vaso-occlusion infarcts the bowel wall, letting Salmonella translocate into the blood, and infarcted bone is easily seeded.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely mechanism of her infection? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: severe abdominal pain during a crisis
steps.x: **Vaso-occlusion** causes bowel ischaemia, so **gut organisms** (Salmonella) translocate. Infarcted bone favours seeding.

elim: No procedure is described.
No ulcer is described.
Hyposplenism mainly affects encapsulated organisms, and does not explain a gut organism.
Salmonella is a gut organism.

steps.x: **A. Bowel infarction allowing gut organisms into the blood.** Sickle cell + Salmonella osteomyelitis = gut infarction + bone infarction.

questions.stem: A 50 year old man has chronic osteomyelitis of the femur with a discharging sinus. At surgery the surgeon removes a loose piece of dead bone and notes it is encased in a thick shell of new bone. His temperature is 37.2°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 134/82 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely nature of the thick shell of new bone?
questions.e: In chronic osteomyelitis the sequestrum of dead bone is surrounded by involucrum of reactive new bone, shielding bacteria, so surgery is needed.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely nature of the thick shell of new bone? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Dead bone = **sequestrum**. New reactive bone around it = **involucrum**. Together they hide bacteria from blood and antibiotics.

elim: Healing bone after a fracture.
An opening in the involucrum through which pus drains.
Bony spur at a joint margin in osteoarthritis.
The dead bone fragment itself.

steps.x: **C. Involucrum.** Sequestrum = dead; involucrum = new shell.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy has a 2 day history of fever and pain in his right distal femur. X-ray of the femur is normal but MRI the same day shows bright signal throughout the metaphyseal marrow. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 100/64 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the different results?
o: Marrow oedema appears before cortical destruction
The MRI shows a tumour, not infection
The X-ray was taken in the wrong place
questions.e: MRI is more sensitive early because it detects bone marrow oedema before the cortical destruction seen on X-ray develops.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely explanation for the different results? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.

clues: X-ray of the femur is normal
bright signal throughout the metaphyseal marrow
steps.x: MRI detects **bone marrow oedema** early; X-ray needs **cortical destruction**, which comes later.

elim: MRI shows tissue water, not organisms.
Fever and a 2 day history point to infection.
The site is clinically localised; early X-rays are often normal.
X-ray shows bone well, but only once it is destroyed.

steps.x: **A. Marrow oedema appears before cortical destruction.** MRI = early marrow oedema; X-ray = late cortical loss.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl has acute osteomyelitis of the proximal tibia after a mild sore throat 2 weeks earlier. There was no injury. Blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus. Her temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 126 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely route of infection?
o: Contiguous spread from a skin ulcer
questions.e: In children, bacteraemia seeds the metaphysis, where the vascular supply is rich but flow is sluggish.

steps.x: The lead-in is: Which is the most likely route of infection? Decide what kind of answer it wants before reading the options.
Positive blood cultures, no wound, a child: **haematogenous** spread to the **metaphysis**, with its rich, sluggish blood flow.

elim: No ulcer is described.
There was no injury.
Joint infection usually follows bone, not the reverse, in this pattern.
Seen in sickle cell disease with Salmonella.

steps.x: **C. Haematogenous seeding of the metaphysis.** Child, no injury, positive cultures = haematogenous seeding.
